# LAR-001
# Chapter 3
# Complete System Architecture

---

# 3.1 Purpose

This chapter defines the complete architectural structure of LoreCanvas.

It explains:

- How every subsystem is organized.
- Why each subsystem exists.
- How information moves through the application.
- Which layers own which responsibilities.
- Which architectural boundaries must never be crossed.

Unlike later chapters, this chapter focuses on the system as a whole rather than individual engines.

---

# 3.2 Architectural Philosophy

LoreCanvas follows **Layered Modular Architecture**.

Each layer performs exactly one category of responsibility.

Higher layers may depend on lower layers.

Lower layers never depend on higher layers.

This creates a one-directional dependency graph that simplifies testing, maintenance, and future expansion.

---

# 3.3 Architectural Layers

LoreCanvas consists of **five architectural layers**.

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            User Experience Layer           │
│          Workspace • Navigation • UI       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Coordination Layer                │
│             Repository Engine              │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│            Domain Layer                    │
│ Node • Card • Link • Query • Template      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Persistence Layer                 │
│             Storage Engine                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          Physical Storage                  │
│ Files • Local Database • Attachments       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

This hierarchy is fixed.

Version 1 should never violate it.

---

# 3.4 Layer Responsibilities

## User Experience Layer

Responsible for:

- displaying information,
- collecting user input,
- arranging windows,
- restoring sessions,
- navigation.

It knows nothing about persistence.

---

## Coordination Layer

Responsible for:

- coordinating operations,
- validating requests,
- managing transactions,
- enforcing architectural rules.

This layer contains the Repository.

---

## Domain Layer

Responsible for modeling the fictional world.

Contains:

- Node Engine
- Card Engine
- Link Engine
- Query Engine
- Template Engine

This layer contains the application's business rules.

---

## Persistence Layer

Responsible only for:

- loading,
- saving,
- backups,
- migration,
- recovery.

No business logic exists here.

---

## Physical Storage Layer

Represents the operating system.

Examples:

- project folders,
- attachments,
- metadata,
- database files.

LoreCanvas communicates with this layer only through the Storage Engine.

---

# 3.5 Architectural Flow

Every user action follows the same path.

```text
User

↓

Workspace

↓

Repository

↓

Domain Engine

↓

Repository

↓

Storage

↓

Disk
```

This sequence never changes.

---

# 3.6 Reverse Flow

Reading data follows a mirrored process.

```text
Disk

↓

Storage

↓

Repository

↓

Domain

↓

Workspace

↓

User
```

---

# 3.7 Why the Repository Sits in the Middle

Many applications allow:

```text
UI

↓

Database
```

LoreCanvas explicitly forbids this.

Instead:

```text
UI

↓

Repository

↓

Everything Else
```

This provides:

- validation,
- consistency,
- transactions,
- logging,
- future synchronization,
- easier testing.

---

# 3.8 Information Ownership

Ownership must always be clear.

| Object | Owner |
|---------|-------|
| Node | Node Engine |
| Card | Card Engine |
| Link | Link Engine |
| Template | Template Engine |
| Query Execution | Query Engine |
| Transactions | Repository |
| Persistence | Storage |
| Session | Workspace |
| Files | Operating System |

No object should have multiple owners.

---

# 3.9 Architectural Boundaries

Each layer has explicit boundaries.

Examples:

### Workspace

May:

- open Nodes,
- request saves,
- display Cards.

May not:

- write directly to Storage,
- modify Links,
- bypass Repository.

---

### Storage

May:

- serialize,
- deserialize,
- backup.

May not:

- validate business rules,
- create Nodes,
- execute Queries.

---

### Query

May:

- traverse data,
- filter,
- sort,
- aggregate.

May not:

- modify Cards,
- modify Links,
- create Nodes.

These rules keep responsibilities isolated.

---

# 3.10 Allowed Dependencies

The dependency graph is intentionally simple.

```text
Workspace
      │
Repository
      │
Node
Card
Link
Query
Template
      │
Storage
```

Dependencies must always point downward.

No engine should depend on Workspace.

Storage must never depend on Node.

The graph should remain acyclic.

---

# 3.11 Architectural Invariants

These rules must always hold true:

1. Every Node belongs to exactly one Project.
2. Every Card belongs to exactly one Node.
3. Every Link connects valid Nodes.
4. Every modification passes through the Repository.
5. Every save passes through the Storage Engine.
6. Queries are read-only.
7. Workspace owns no project data.
8. Storage performs no business validation.

Breaking any invariant is considered an architectural defect.

---

# 3.12 Failure Isolation

A failure in one subsystem should not automatically propagate.

Examples:

- A Workspace crash should not corrupt project data.
- A failed save should not invalidate in-memory objects.
- A plugin failure (future) should not affect the Repository.
- A malformed Template should not damage existing Nodes.

Each engine should fail independently whenever possible.

---

# 3.13 Version 1 Simplicity

The architecture intentionally excludes:

- distributed systems,
- networking,
- online synchronization,
- background collaboration,
- AI orchestration.

These features are future extensions.

Version 1 remains intentionally local and deterministic.

---

# 3.14 Architecture Decision Record (ADR-001)

**Decision:** Adopt a layered modular architecture.

**Reasoning:**

- Clear separation of concerns.
- High testability.
- Easier maintenance.
- Predictable dependencies.
- Better scalability.
- Future compatibility with AI and cloud features.

**Alternatives Considered:**

- Monolithic document model.
- MVC without engine separation.
- Direct UI-to-storage communication.

**Outcome:**

Layered modular architecture chosen.

---

# 3.15 Why This Matters

The architecture is the foundation upon which every feature of LoreCanvas is built.

By separating user interaction, coordination, domain logic, and persistence into distinct layers, the system becomes easier to understand, test, extend, and maintain. More importantly, it ensures that future capabilities, whether AI, cloud synchronization, or plugins, can be introduced without compromising the stability of the core application.

---

# My review of this chapter

I think we've reached a new level of specificity.

However, I also see an opportunity to make LAR-001 even stronger.

## I'd like to introduce a new artifact: **Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)**

Rather than sprinkling one or two ADRs through the document, I propose creating an appendix that records every major architectural decision:

- ADR-001: Layered Modular Architecture
- ADR-002: Repository as Single Source of Truth
- ADR-003: Separation of Nodes and Cards
- ADR-004: Offline-First Version 1
- ADR-005: Links as First-Class Objects
- ADR-006: Queries are Read-Only
- ADR-007: Plugins Designed but Deferred
- ...and so on.

Each ADR would explain not only **what** we decided, but **why**, what alternatives we considered, and what trade-offs we accepted.

This is a common practice in mature software projects because it preserves architectural reasoning. Years later, when someone asks, *"Why is LoreCanvas built this way?"*, the answer isn't hidden in old chats or commit history. It's documented in the architecture itself. I think adding a formal ADR appendix will make LAR-001 feel like a professional engineering manual rather than just a technical specification.

## ADR-003
### Separation of Node and Card

**Status**
Accepted

**Context**

Traditional applications combine identity and information into one object.

```
Character
├── Name
├── Biography
├── Inventory
├── Appearance
├── Relationships
└── ...
```

As projects grow, this becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.

**Decision**

Separate identity from knowledge.

```
Node
      │
      ├── Biography Card
      ├── Appearance Card
      ├── Inventory Card
      ├── Personality Card
      └── History Card
```

**Benefits**

- Modular information.
- Easier Templates.
- Better Queries.
- Independent editing.
- Cleaner architecture.

**Trade-offs**

- Slightly more objects.
- Repository coordination required.

**Alternatives Considered**

- Single document model.
- Embedded notes.
- Wiki-style pages.

**Reason for Rejection**

Reduced flexibility and weaker scalability.

---

That keeps the chapter readable while preserving the reasoning.

# Chapter 4

## Project Architecture

This chapter becomes the root of the domain.

---

## Purpose

A Project represents an entire fictional universe managed by LoreCanvas.

It is the highest-level domain object and the primary unit of persistence.

Every object stored within LoreCanvas belongs to exactly one Project.

Projects define the boundaries of identity, ownership, persistence, and discovery.

---

## Responsibilities

The Project is responsible for:

- Establishing the ownership boundary for all data.
- Defining the root namespace for Nodes.
- Containing Cards, Links, Templates, Queries, and Attachments.
- Providing metadata for persistence and restoration.
- Acting as the root object loaded and saved by the Storage Engine.

---

## Non-Responsibilities

A Project does **not**:

- Perform Queries.
- Validate Links.
- Manage Workspace state.
- Store business logic.
- Execute Templates.

These responsibilities belong to dedicated engines.

---

## Ownership Hierarchy

```text
Project
│
├── Nodes
│     ├── Cards
│     └── Links (through Link Engine)
│
├── Templates
│
├── Queries
│
├── Attachments
│
└── Metadata
```

The Project owns these collections conceptually. Individual engines remain responsible for managing their contents.

---

## Identity

Every Project has:

- Project UUID
- Project Name
- Description
- Creation Date
- Last Modified Date
- Version
- Author (optional)
- Metadata

Project identifiers remain stable throughout the life of the Project.

---

## Scope Boundary

Objects cannot belong to more than one Project.

Cross-project Links are not supported in Version 1.

Cross-project Queries are not supported in Version 1.

Templates are local to their Project unless explicitly exported and imported.

---

## Lifecycle

```text
Create
   ↓
Initialize
   ↓
Active
   ↓
Save
   ↓
Close
   ↓
Archive
   ↓
Restore
   ↓
Delete
```

Deletion permanently removes the Project and all associated data after confirmation. Recovery behavior will be defined by the Storage chapter.

---

## Invariants

The following rules must always hold:

1. Every Node belongs to exactly one Project.
2. Every Card belongs to a Node within the same Project.
3. Every Link connects Nodes within the same Project.
4. Every Template belongs to exactly one Project.
5. Every Query executes within a single Project context.
6. Every Attachment belongs to exactly one Project.

Violation of these rules constitutes an architectural defect.

---

## Dependency Rules

The Project depends on no other domain object.

Instead, other domain objects exist within the Project boundary.

This makes the Project the **root aggregate** of the domain model.

---

# Why this chapter matters

This is one of those changes that seems small but improves the architecture.

Previously, the Node felt like the root object.

But after reviewing the entire system, the Project is clearly the true root. Every other domain concept exists inside it.

By making the Project explicit, we gain a cleaner mental model, simpler ownership rules, and a more natural place to define persistence boundaries.

---

# One more architectural improvement

As we've refined the architecture, I've noticed another opportunity.

At the moment, we often use the word "Engine" for every subsystem. That's fine, but not every subsystem behaves like an engine.

I propose introducing three categories:

| Category | Purpose | Examples |
|----------|---------|----------|
| **Core Models** | Represent domain concepts | Project, Node, Card, Link |
| **Engines** | Perform operations on Core Models | Query Engine, Template Engine, Repository, Storage |
| **Services** | Provide supporting capabilities without owning domain data | Validation Service, Backup Service, Import/Export Service (future) |

This distinction doesn't change the current architecture, but it gives us a clearer vocabulary as LoreCanvas grows. It also avoids calling every component an "engine" when some are fundamentally data models and others are operational systems.

I recommend we adopt this terminology now so the remainder of Volume I stays internally consistent.

# LAR-001
# Volume I
## Part II - Core Domain

---

# Chapter 5
# Node Model Specification

> **Notice the name change.**
>
> I intentionally changed **Node Engine** to **Node Model**.
>
> A Node doesn't "do" anything.
>
> It **exists**.
>
> The Repository and Query Engine operate on Nodes, but the Node itself is simply a domain model.
>
> I think this terminology is much more accurate.

---

# 5.1 Purpose

The Node Model defines **identity**.

Every entity that exists within a Project is represented by exactly one Node.

The Node is the canonical source of identity throughout LoreCanvas.

All references within the application ultimately resolve to a Node.

---

# 5.2 Design Goals

The Node Model is designed to satisfy the following goals:

- Stable identity throughout the life of a Project.
- Minimal stored information.
- Independence from presentation.
- Independence from persistence implementation.
- Independence from knowledge content.
- Compatibility with future expansion.

These goals ensure that a Node remains lightweight, durable, and reusable.

---

# 5.3 Core Principle

A Node represents **existence**, not **description**.

A Node answers:

> **"What exists?"**

It does **not** answer:

- What does it look like?
- What happened to it?
- Who does it know?
- Where is it located?
- What powers does it possess?

Those questions are answered by Cards and Links.

---

# 5.4 Node Structure

Every Node shall contain the following required fields:

| Field | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| UUID | Permanent unique identifier |
| Type | Category of entity |
| Display Name | Human-readable name |
| Status | Active, Archived, Deleted |
| Created At | Creation timestamp |
| Modified At | Last modification timestamp |
| Project UUID | Owning Project reference |

No additional fields are mandatory.

This keeps the Node lightweight and focused.

---

# 5.5 Node Types

Version 1 provides a predefined set of Node Types.

These types are used for organization, templates, and queries.

The initial types include:

### Characters

Represents individual fictional people or beings.

---

### Locations

Represents places of any scale.

Examples:

- Buildings
- Cities
- Forests
- Continents

---

### Organizations

Represents structured groups.

Examples:

- Guilds
- Kingdoms
- Governments
- Companies

---

### Species

Represents biological or fictional races.

---

### Items

Represents physical objects.

Examples:

- Weapons
- Relics
- Artifacts
- Books

---

### Events

Represents occurrences within the fictional world.

Examples:

- Wars
- Births
- Catastrophes
- Festivals

---

### Concepts

Represents abstract entities.

Examples:

- Religions
- Magic Systems
- Languages
- Laws
- Political Systems

---

# 5.6 Node Identity

Node identity is immutable.

The following properties must never change after creation:

- UUID
- Creation timestamp
- Original Project ownership

The following properties may change:

- Display Name
- Type (subject to validation)
- Status

---

# 5.7 Ownership

Nodes are owned by the Project.

Cards are owned by Nodes.

Links reference Nodes.

Queries discover Nodes.

Templates create Nodes.

The ownership chain is therefore:

```text
Project
   │
   └── Node
         │
         ├── Cards
         └── Referenced by Links
```

---

# 5.8 Lifecycle

Every Node progresses through the following lifecycle:

```text
Created
   ↓
Validated
   ↓
Registered
   ↓
Active
   ↓
Archived
   ↓
Restored
   ↓
Deleted
```

Transitions must occur through the Repository.

Direct state changes are prohibited.

---

# 5.9 Node Status

Each Node exists in one of three states:

| Status | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Active | Fully available for editing and queries |
| Archived | Hidden by default but recoverable |
| Deleted | Pending permanent removal |

The Deleted state is an intermediate state that supports recovery before irreversible deletion.

---

# 5.10 Relationships to Other Models

The Node Model does not contain:

- Card content
- Link definitions
- Query definitions
- Template definitions

Instead, it participates in relationships managed by those systems.

This separation prevents circular dependencies and keeps the model cohesive.

---

# 5.11 Constraints

The following constraints are mandatory:

- A Node must belong to exactly one Project.
- A Node must have exactly one UUID.
- A Node cannot exist without a valid Project.
- A Node cannot own another Node.
- A Node cannot directly reference itself through ownership.

These constraints define the integrity of the model.

---

# 5.12 Acceptance Criteria

The Node Model is considered correctly implemented when:

- Every Node has a stable identity.
- Nodes remain lightweight regardless of project size.
- Identity is independent of descriptive content.
- All references resolve through UUIDs.
- Lifecycle transitions occur only through the Repository.
- Ownership rules are enforced.

---

# Review of the Node Model

Now that we've written this chapter, I think it's already much closer to the level of detail expected in a professional architecture specification.

However, I also see one architectural question we should answer **before** moving on to the Card Model:

### Should a Node know what Cards it owns?

Right now we've assumed:

```text
Node
   │
   ├── Biography Card
   ├── Appearance Card
   └── Inventory Card
```

But there's another valid architecture:

```text
Node

Card
   └── references Node UUID
```

In the second design, the Node doesn't maintain a list of Cards at all. Instead, the Card Model references its parent Node, and the Repository resolves those relationships when needed.

This choice has implications for performance, ownership clarity, persistence, and future features like undo/redo and synchronization.

I don't want to answer it by instinct. I think we should evaluate both approaches on their merits before locking it into the architecture, because once it's part of LAR-001, it becomes a foundational decision that many later chapters will depend on.
